discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the opening of neutrino astronomy with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led IceCube, a cubic-kilometre detector built in the Antarctic ice, which opened a new window on the Universe. In 2013 IceCube discovered a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos. In 2017 a real-time IceCube alert, followed up by gamma-ray and optical telescopes, linked a neutrino to the flaring blazar TXS 0506+056. This was the first multi-messenger identification of a cosmic-ray accelerator. Later results found neutrino emission from the Galactic plane and from the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068. These give direct evidence about where hadrons are accelerated, a question gamma rays alone cannot settle. IceCube's low-latency alert infrastructure changed how astronomers and particle physicists work together, much as gravitational-wave alerts did. Halzen's vision and his persistence over decades created neutrino astronomy as an observational science, and it is now a central pillar of multi-messenger astrophysics.
